prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I have moved from B032 to B018 as my preferred configuration. The decisive point is what the first-round exchange showed about the shape of each case. For optical lattice clocks, the idea and its decisive demonstration sit in the same two names: Katori proposed and first realised the magic-wavelength lattice, which cancels the light shift of the clock transition while holding many atoms free of Doppler and recoil broadening, and Ye carried the lattice clock to record accuracy and many-body-limited operation. The result is measured, not inferred, near 1e-18, and it has been reproduced and compared in several independent laboratories. It also yields consequences that are quantitative and still growing: relativistic geodesy, tests of constancy of fundamental constants, ultralight dark-matter searches and the basis for a redefinition of the second. The lattice step is a trapping concept, not a frequency-measurement concept, so it is separable from the comb (2005) and from ion control (2012). As a theorist who works on quantum devices I find a concept validated by precision measurement more persuasive than a blueprint whose realisation is credited to others. The citation should stay narrow, naming the magic-wavelength lattice clock, so that it does not claim the whole optical-clock lineage.
statement.case_against: My earlier hesitation about B018 was that cooling (1997), the comb (2005) and ion control (2012) lie close by, and that a prize for precision could read as metrology rather than a discovery in physics. I now think the first concern is answered by the narrow citation. The second remains partly open: the committee should be explicit that it is rewarding a new capability whose measured consequences are physical, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so part of the case rests on an anticipated outcome. The two-name credit also leaves out real contributors such as Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and ion-clock groups, and I cannot verify the priority sequence between early lattice proposals and the first operating clocks. Against my own former choice, B032 remains a strong theoretical case, but its credit points to a blueprint whose realisation was largely credited elsewhere, and it overlaps with B015.

responses.point: Kroll asked what pushed lattice clocks down in my own thinking, and whether it was the earlier recognition of cooling and the comb, which is the concern he raises against his own first choice.
responses.response: Yes, that was the main reason, together with a habit of my field of weighing proposals above instruments. Having reread the exchange I think the overlap argument is weaker than I made it. Laser cooling made the atoms available and the comb made optical frequencies countable, but the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate trapping idea that determines what accuracy is reachable at all, and your own description of it as a concept that was proposed before it was realised matches that. I therefore treat the earlier prizes as foundations and not as coverage. I agree with you that a two-name credit is bought partly by omission, and I would manage that through the wording of the citation, not by adding names beyond the limit.

responses.point: Lindroth noted that honouring the Cirac-Zoller proposals alone would leave the two-qubit gate demonstrations by Blatt, Wineland, Monroe and others unrecognised, and that B032 overlaps with B015; she also noted she has not verified the lattice priority sequence.
responses.response: You persuaded me on the first point. In round 1 I defended a theory-only prize by saying the 2012 citation did not cover the gate proposal, but the other side of that argument is that the demonstrations are not covered either, and a prize for the proposal alone would look unbalanced. Adding experimentalists would take the configuration to at least four names, which the limit forbids, and I said earlier that dropping one theorist would be less fair. For that reason I am no longer pressing B032. On priority, I share your uncertainty about the sequence of early lattice proposals and the first operating clocks, and I do not think anyone at the table has verified it. I would accept B018 on the stated Katori-Ye attribution while recording that caveat.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B020 to B018 on the ground that the proposal and decisive demonstration share two names, and noted that B032 is less self-contained, with the same pair appearing in B015.
responses.response: I agree with the self-containedness point, and it carries real weight with me. A prize should be explicable in one citation without relying on experiments credited in a different part of the list. B032 cannot do that, because the Cirac-Zoller cold-atom proposals and the Bloch-Greiner experiments are one story across B032 and B015. I disagree with one thing: you defer to others on the technical claims about systematic uncertainties. I cannot independently check them either, and my judgment rests on the reproduction in several laboratories more than on my own assessment of the error budget.

responses.point: The chair asks whether a new observational window such as IceCube should outrank a measured precision advance, and whether any two- or three-name IceCube credit can be defended against the collaboration and AMANDA precursors.
responses.response: I keep B007 as an alternative and do not dispute that the diffuse flux is secure. I do not think the discovery character of a new messenger automatically outweighs a measured advance, and I read the question as one of attribution as much as of kind. In a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and Baikal as precursors and Yoshida's omission from a two-name credit, I cannot defend a compact configuration as easily as I can for Katori and Ye. If colleagues can fix the IceCube credit convincingly I would move B007 above B032 as my second choice, but today I rank B018 above it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads lattice clocks as a discovery in physics or as precision metrology, and whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay a prize.
Whether the Katori-Ye credit is separable enough from Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and ion-clock groups; I rely on recollection of the priority sequence and have not verified it.

Whether I was right to give weight to the 2012 prize as an argument against B032, and whether the committee would take a theory-only prize for Cirac and Zoller if it treated B032 and B015 as one achievement.
Whether my earlier low placement of B018 reflected scientific judgment or the habits of my own field, which is why I let the round-1 arguments of others move me.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits and circuit and waveguide QED, so I would recuse myself from any discussion of B008 (circuit QED). Chalmers colleagues were associated with the 2025 prize, and I have publicly named Devoret as one reason I entered the field. Olsson is also a Chalmers colleague, and I note that this does not bear on B018. I know of no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, Cirac, Zoller or the IceCube candidates. I am now no longer advocating a candidate in my own research area, which reduces the proximity concern.
